# Exportação de relatórios em background

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estado** | Implementado |
| **Autores** | Time de Relatórios |
| **Revisores** | Marina Prado (Plataforma) |
| **Criado em** | 2026-01-12 |
| **Última atualização** | 2026-03-03 |

## Visão geral

Relatórios grandes eram gerados dentro da request da API e estouravam o timeout de 30s do gateway. Este documento descreve o serviço que gera esses relatórios fora da request: a API enfileira o pedido, um worker gera o arquivo e o usuário baixa quando fica pronto.

## Objetivos e fora de escopo

Objetivos:

- Nenhuma exportação falha por timeout do gateway.
- O usuário recebe o link de download em até 5 minutos para relatórios de até 1 milhão de linhas.

Fora de escopo:

- Agendamento recorrente de relatórios.
- Formatos além de CSV.

## Solução

A API grava o pedido na tabela `export_jobs` e responde 202 com o id do job. Um worker lê os jobs pendentes, gera o CSV e grava o arquivo no disco local dele, em `/var/exports/<job_id>.csv`. O endpoint `GET /exports/<job_id>/download` é servido pelo próprio worker, que lê o arquivo do disco e devolve.

Os arquivos ficam 7 dias no disco; um cron do worker apaga os mais antigos.

## Trade-offs da solução escolhida

- ✓ Nenhuma dependência nova: só a tabela de jobs e o disco que o worker já tem.
- ✓ Download sem custo de transferência de storage externo.
- ✗ O arquivo só existe no worker que o gerou. A solução assume um único worker.
- ✗ Se o disco do worker se perde, os arquivos dos últimos 7 dias se perdem junto.

## Alternativas consideradas

**Gravar os arquivos num bucket de object storage.** Tiraria a dependência do disco do worker, mas exigia credenciais e política de retenção novas. Com um único worker previsto, o time considerou o custo desnecessário.

**Não fazer nada.** Descartada: as exportações acima de 200 mil linhas falhavam em toda tentativa.

## Questões em aberto

Nenhuma.

Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-1000/-home-cassiobotaro-Projetos-skills/fb3cd090-d616-4f36-afbf-c763a9b2fa6e/scratchpad/border/p10/project/.claude/skills/technical-writing

# Technical writing

A technical document works when its reader can act after one reading: run the service,
clear the alert, review the change. Two things decide that more than style does. The
document does one job for one reader, and every sentence says who does what.

## The contract

1. **Every verb has an actor.** For each verb, the sentence says who or what performs the
   action: a person, a team, a component, a command, the reader. "The payload is
   validated" withholds a fact the reader needs: which service to open, whom to page,
   whether the step is theirs. The reader fills the hole with a guess. Write the actor as
   the subject of an active verb: "The gateway validates the payload". Section 4 has the
   test and the few passives that stay.

2. **Look the actor up, never pick one.** A passive is a question: who does this? The
   answer is in the code, the configuration, the existing docs, or the conversation, so
   read them. When none of them answers, the question goes to the user. A plausible
   component written as the actor is a fabrication that reads like knowledge. The same
   rule covers every command, flag, path, default, version, and output: copy it from the
   repository or from a run of the command, never from how such tools usually work. It
   also covers behavior: write what the code does. A likely cause, or what systems of
   this kind usually do, is marked as a guess or left out.

3. **One reader, one job.** Fix who reads and what they do next before writing a
   sentence (section 1). A document does one of four jobs (section 2). A page that
   teaches, instructs, lists, and argues at once serves no reader well.

4. **The house governs.** A style guide, a template, or the docs already in the repository
   set the terms, the heading style, and the structure. A new document follows the
   language of the repository's docs directory (`docs/`, `doc/`, or the like) when there
   is one with documents in it, and the language of the conversation otherwise. A
   language the user names wins over both. In a revision, the author's language,
   structure, voice, and facts stay.

## Writing a document

### 1. Fix the reader and the task

Settle two things from the request and the repository: who reads (their role, and what
they already know about this system) and what they must be able to do after reading. The
document holds what the task needs minus what the reader already knows. The usual failure
is the writer's own knowledge: a term the team uses every day is unknown one team away.

Do not interview. Ask only when two plausible readers would get very different documents
and nothing decides between them. Otherwise write for the most likely reader and name that
reader in one line of the reply, so that one word corrects it.

### 2. Choose the job

Ask what the reader is doing when they open the page.

| The reader is | Job | It holds | It leaves out |
|---|---|---|---|
| learning by doing | Tutorial | one path that works, a visible result at every step | options, alternatives, explanation beyond a clause |
| working toward a goal | How-to guide | the steps to that goal, for a competent reader | teaching, background, the full list of options |
| looking up a fact mid-task | Reference | description only, complete, in the shape of the thing described | instructions, opinion, history |
| trying to understand | Explanation | context, reasons, alternatives, consequences | steps, exhaustive detail |

When the material spans two jobs, write two documents and link them. A README is the one
mixed page: a short piece of each job, with links to the rest. Before writing any of
these, or a runbook, release notes, a changelog entry, a pull request description, or a
commit message, read the entry for that document in `references/documents.md`.

### 3. Collect the facts

Read the source before drafting: the code paths the document describes, the build and
task files, the configuration, the existing docs. For each action the document will
mention, find its actor now. Run a command to confirm it only when the run changes
nothing (a read, `--help`, a dry run). Keep a list of what you could not confirm.

When the repository leaves a hole the document cannot work around (what the service is
for, who is on call, which environment the steps target), ask before writing: two to four
questions, batched, in the conversation language. Do not ask what you can read yourself.
When the user wants the document before they can answer, write it and mark each hole
where it falls, as a `TODO` that says what is missing. Never paper over a hole, and list
every one in the reply.

### 4. Draft, then run the actor pass

Draft with the rules of the next section. Then go through the draft one verb at a time
and ask "who or what does this?" The sentence has to answer.

Rebecca Johnson's test finds the passives fast: if "by zombies" fits after the verb, the
verb is passive ("por zumbis" in Portuguese). "The cache is invalidated [by zombies] on
deploy." Zombies fit because the sentence never said who invalidates the cache, and that
missing name is what you now look up. The test catches only the first of the six places
where the actor hides, so the question still goes to every verb:

- **A passive without its agent.** "The cache is invalidated on deploy" becomes "The
  deploy job invalidates the cache".
- **A noun that swallowed the verb.** "After validation of the token" becomes "After the
  gateway validates the token".
- **A subject that means nothing.** "It is recommended to", "there is a retry", "é
  necessário configurar". Write who recommends, what retries, who configures.
- **A catch-all actor.** "The system", "the application", "the process", when the system
  has several parts. Name the part.
- **An instruction written as a description.** "The variable must be set" becomes "Set
  the variable". The actor is the reader, so use the imperative.
- **In Portuguese, the forms with "se".** "Envia-se", "configura-se", "deve-se" hide the
  actor as "é enviado" does.

Two passives stay:

- **The actor is unknown, and the text says so.** "The index was dropped at 14:02. The
  audit log does not record by whom."
- **The verb describes a state, and no reader would ask "by whom?"** "The service is
  written in Go." "This endpoint is deprecated."

A passive that names its actor with "by" is rewritten like any other. When the paragraph
follows one thing through the system and that thing should stay at the front of the
sentence, give it an active verb: "The request then goes to the gateway, which signs it".

`references/actors.md` has before and after pairs for each case, in English and in
Portuguese. Read it when a sentence resists the rewrite, when the document is in
Portuguese, or when you review a text you did not write.

### 5. Apply `unslop`, then check

When the `unslop` skill is installed, invoke it on the prose you wrote or rewrote in this
turn, after the actor pass. It owns the catalog of machine-writing patterns, and this
skill does not repeat that catalog. A fact that skill finds missing is a question for the
user (contract 2). Then check:

- Every verb has an actor, and each passive left is one of the two that stay.
- Every command, flag, path, name, and output exists in the repository or came from a run.
- The first paragraph alone tells the reader what this is and whether to read on.
- The document does one job. Material for another job is a link.
- Each thing has one name, and it is the name the code uses.
- A final read as the reader fixed in step 1, from the top, doing what the page says.

## The rules

### The document

- Lead with the point. The first paragraph says what the thing is and what the reader
  gets from the page, in words they would search for. Many readers stop there.
- State what the document covers, and what it leaves out that a reader would expect to
  find. Put prerequisites before the first step.
- A heading says what its section holds. A heading for a task starts with a verb.
- Cut what the reader's task does not need. Link to a detail instead of repeating it.

### The paragraph

- The first sentence states the point of the paragraph. One topic per paragraph.
- Start a sentence with what the reader already has, and end it with what is new. The
  end of the sentence is where the reader puts the emphasis.
- Use a numbered list for a sequence, bullets for parallel items, a table for items
  compared on the same attributes, and prose for reasoning, because a list drops the
  connectives. Introduce a list with a full sentence and keep its items parallel.

### The sentence

- Actor, verb, object, in that order, with the subject next to its verb.
- Let the verb carry the action: "validates", not "performs the validation of".
- One idea per sentence. Put the condition before the instruction: "To roll back, run…",
  "If the check fails, restart the worker".
- Present tense. Address the reader as "you", in the form of address the house uses.
- Prefer the positive form, and never stack negatives: "the job retries once the lock
  is free", not "the job does not retry unless the lock is not held".
- Write the number with its unit, and the exact name. "Slow" and "some errors" cannot be
  acted on, and "p95 above 800 ms" and "`ERR_QUOTA`" can.

### The words

- One name per thing, everywhere, and the name the code uses. A second name reads as a
  second thing.
- Define a term where it first appears. Spell an acronym out once, and only when the
  document uses it several times.
- "It", "this", and "they" point at one noun the reader has just read. Otherwise repeat
  the noun.
- Identifiers, commands, paths, and values go in code font, spelled as in the source.
- Leave "simply", "just", "easy", and "obviously" out of instructions. They tell the
  reader who is stuck that the fault is theirs.

### Procedures and samples

- One action per step, numbered, each step starting with an imperative verb. Say where
  before what: "In `config/app.yaml`, set…".
- Put a warning before the step it guards.
- After a step with a result the reader can check, show that result.
- A command block holds only what the reader types, with no prompt character. Mark a
  placeholder as `<name>` and say what replaces it.
- A sample runs as written, is as small as the point allows, and says how to run it and
  what it prints.

## Revising and reviewing

**"Improve", "revise", "update".** Edit the file. Keep the author's structure, voice, and
every fact (contract 4), and change what the rules above call for. A passive whose actor
the repository does not give stays as it is and becomes a question in the reply. Do not
delete the sentence and do not guess.

**"Review".** Report before editing, in two groups: questions for the author (an actor
or a fact that only they know, a reader the document never settles) and proposed edits,
each with its reason. Quote the sentence. Apply what the user chooses.

## When another skill calls this one

Apply the actor pass (step 4) and the rules for the sentence and the words to the prose
that skill wrote in this turn, before `unslop` runs. Structure, headings, templates, and
tool-parsed text belong to the calling skill and stay as they are. An actor nobody
established goes where that skill puts its open questions. Add no report of your own.

## Deliver

- **A new document.** Write it where the repository keeps its docs and report the path.
- **A revision.** Edit in place, report the path, and say in at most three lines what
  changed.
- **A short text** (a pull request description, a commit message). Reply with the text
  ready to paste. Do not post or commit it unless the user asked.

After the result, list only what applies: the reader you assumed, the questions left
open, and the commands you did not run. Do not summarize the document.

## Reference files

| File | Read it when |
|---|---|
| `references/documents.md` | Before writing or reviewing a specific kind of document: what each one must hold, its order, and its usual failure. |
| `references/actors.md` | A sentence resists the actor pass, the document is in Portuguese, or you review a text you did not write. |

## Attribution

The layered structure follows the `technical-writing` skill of
[pstack](https://github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack) by Lauren Tan, licensed MIT.
The rule that every verb has an actor follows Tanya Reilly's *The Staff Engineer's Path*.
The four jobs are Daniele Procida's Diátaxis. The rules condense Google's Technical
Writing courses and developer documentation style guide, the Microsoft Writing Style
Guide, the US federal plain language guidelines, Write the Docs, and George Gopen and
Judith Swan's "The Science of Scientific Writing". The "by zombies" test is Rebecca
Johnson's. See `NOTICE.md`.

---
name: design-doc
license: MIT
description: >
  Write and review software design documents through interactive discovery: ask the
  user targeted questions about the problem, the trade-offs, the alternatives, and the
  impacted teams, then write (or improve) a clear, trade-off-focused Markdown design
  doc. Use this skill whenever the user wants to plan or document a technical design
  before (or while) building it, or to improve a design document that already exists —
  "write a design doc", "review my design doc", "document the approach for this new
  service", "help me think through this design before we build", "the team needs to
  align on this design" — even if they never say "design doc".
---

# Design Docs

You are an expert in writing and reviewing design documents — the informal docs the
builders of a system write *before* building it: the implementation strategy and the
main decisions, with emphasis on the trade-offs. Teams write them to find design
problems while changes are cheap, to build consensus, and to remember *why* the system
is the way it is. Your method is **interactive discovery**: a design doc records its
author's reasoning, so the heart of the work is drawing that reasoning out of the user
with the right questions and writing it down clearly. The document is theirs; the
questions are yours.

The deliverable of every invocation is Markdown on disk: a new design doc, edits to
the document under review, or an update to a document whose design has changed.

## The contract

1. **Trade-offs are the soul of the document.** A doc that records only what will be
   built — no costs, no alternatives, no why — loses all value the moment the code
   exists. Never jump from problem to solution: show *why* the chosen solution
   satisfies the goals better than the alternatives, and state plainly what got worse
   in exchange for what got better. A solution presented with zero downsides is a
   sales pitch — treat it as a red flag and dig for the cost that was accepted.

2. **Record, don't invent.** Never fabricate metrics, constraints, stakeholders,
   alternatives, or rationale that the user (or the repository) did not establish.
   When substance is missing, ask targeted questions in the conversation language —
   see "Discover the substance" below. Polishing the user's reasoning into clear prose
   is your job; supplying missing facts is not. This binds hardest inside diagrams,
   where the notation asks for a technology under a box or a protocol on an arrow the
   author never gave: leave the slot empty and ask (see `references/diagrams.md`).

   Invention also arrives as *inference* — a claim nobody made, derived from one they did.
   Watch every word that claims exclusivity or universality (*the only*, *the sole*,
   *always*, *never*, and their equivalents in the writing language): they turn an
   unstated absence into a fact. "There is no per-client limit today" does not license
   "manual intervention was the only brake" — a global throttle or a WAF rule are equally
   unmentioned, and a reviewer who knows about the WAF now distrusts the whole document.
   Write what was established ("there is no automatic per-client containment today") or
   make the absence a question.

   Inference also arrives as a *consequence*: what must be true now, deduced from what
   the user said changed. Told that sessions moved from process memory to a shared
   cache, do not write that "a restart no longer logs anyone out" or that "every
   instance reads the same session" — the user said where the data went, not how the
   rest of the system behaves since. The day you write is likewise not the day the
   change happened. The test is mechanical: a fact cannot be both asserted in one
   section and asked in Open questions. If you are asking it, delete the assertion.

3. **The template governs; without one, sections are suggestions.** When the user
   supplies a template — or the repository's design docs already follow one — its
   sections are the document's contract: cover every one, in the template's order, and
   when the conversation hasn't given you the substance for a section, ask the user to
   fill it rather than skipping it or stuffing it with boilerplate (a hole where Risks
   should be reads as "nobody thought about risks"). Without a template, draw from the
   catalog below by what brings clarity — recommended minimum: a header, the problem,
   and the solution, written around trade-offs — and *suggest* additions rather than
   demand them. Either way, never fabricate content to fill a section. A governing
   template is a floor, not a ceiling: substance the template has nowhere to put (goals,
   alternatives they weighed) gets its own section rather than being dropped, with the
   house skeleton and order kept intact and the deviation named to the user, so it is
   theirs to accept. This contract binds what *you* write; a review never audits a
   document for presence of sections — see "Reviewing an existing document".

4. **Follow the document's context.** When reviewing, keep the document's existing
   language, structure, and voice — improve the doc the author wrote, don't replace it
   with the doc you would have written. When creating, write in the language of the
   conversation unless asked otherwise.

5. **Right-size the document.** The effort should be proportional to the ambiguity of
   the problem. A 1–3 page mini-doc is perfectly fine for incremental work; a doc
   growing past 10–20 pages is a signal the problem should be split. This skill writes
   design docs, nothing else: if what the user actually has is a single already-made
   decision with no design to discover, say so instead of manufacturing a design doc
   around it — that is an ADR (the `adr` skill when it is installed, the team's decision
   log otherwise). The same holds when nothing is ambiguous: if neither the problem nor
   the solution leaves a choice open, the document can only be an implementation manual,
   and the code review already covers that. Say so in a sentence and ask once whether
   something is in fact undecided, or whether the team's process requires a doc anyway;
   if it does, write a terse mini-doc and manufacture no alternatives or risks to pad it.

## Writing a new document

### 1. Find the shape

Template precedence: a user-supplied template governs (contract 3); otherwise existing
design docs in the repository (`docs/design/`, `design/`, `docs/`) define a house
structure — treat it exactly like a user-supplied template, since a collection in two
formats is worse than either alone; only without either, use the default section
catalog below, selecting only the sections this particular problem needs.

Put the doc where the repository already keeps design docs. If there is no precedent,
ask the user where to save it (suggesting `docs/design/` is fine). Derive the filename
from the title as a short slug; if the existing collection uses IDs (e.g.
`DD-2026-014`), continue the convention.

### 2. Discover the substance — the heart of the work

An honest design doc needs: **the problem** (what hurts today, why solving it matters
now), **the boundaries** (what the work will achieve — ideally measurable — and what
is deliberately out of scope), **the constraints** (what cannot change: a legacy
system, a host platform, a contract with another team — in a heavily constrained design
they explain why every option is imperfect), **the solution** (concrete enough to evaluate), **the
accepted costs** (what got worse in exchange for what got better), **the alternatives**
(what else was considered, including "do nothing", and why the chosen path won), and
**the blast radius** (who outside the team is impacted — security, infrastructure,
other systems' load, compatibility).

The accepted costs are their own question, not a rider on the solution question. Asking
"what does the design look like?" reliably gets you a description with no downsides in
it — contract 1 calls that a red flag, so ask for the cost directly: "what does this
approach make worse, and what did the team decide to live with?"

If the user's prompt and the repository already provide these, do not interrogate the
user — write. For what's missing, ask 2–5 targeted questions in the conversation
language *before* creating the file: this interview is where the document's value is
created, and when the essentials are missing, the deliverable of the turn is your
questions, not a skeleton of placeholder sections.

When a template governs the document, also ask one question per template section the
conversation hasn't filled (contract 3) — an unfilled required section is a question to
the user, never a silent omission. Without a template, don't block on the optional: a
missing deployment plan is a section to skip or an open question to record, not an
interrogation to conduct.

Don't ask what you can verify yourself (current architecture, existing conventions).
`references/sections.md` pairs each section with the question to ask when its
substance is missing.

### 3. Write

- **Write plainly and in the active voice.** Name the actor: "the worker pulls jobs
  from the queue" says who does what; "jobs are pulled from the queue" hides the actor a
  design doc exists to pin down. Passive constructions and nominalizations ("a decision
  was reached to…") read as evasive and bury responsibility — prefer short, concrete
  sentences that read the way a person would explain the design out loud.
- **Keep the typography plain.** Generated prose leans on a handful of tics that a reader
  recognises at a glance, so avoid them: em dashes as a default connector (one or two in
  the whole document is the ceiling — use commas, periods, or parentheses, and a colon
  for list labels and headings); a colon that sets up a reveal ("The central trade-off:
  the user loses…" — write it as a sentence); bold on a single word for emphasis; an
  opening paragraph that announces what the document contains; and the same sentence
  shape recurring as a gap marker ("the team has not yet decided…" in every section —
  state the gap once, in Open questions, and link to it).
- **Run the `unslop` skill when it is installed**: once the document is on disk, invoke
  that skill on the prose you wrote or rewrote in this turn, then do the self-review on
  its result. It owns the full catalog of these tics, and the two bullets above are the

author's reasoning, so the heart of the work is drawing that reasoning out of the user

   satisfies the goals better than the alternatives, and state plainly what got worse
   in exchange for what got better. A solution presented with zero downsides is a
   sales pitch — treat it as a red flag and dig for the cost that was accepted.

   alternatives, or rationale that the user (or the repository) did not establish.

Esse doc já está em produção, então não vou editar o corpo dele. Ele é o registro de por que o serviço foi construído daquele jeito. O fluxo do `design-doc` para mudança em design já entregue é este:

- Escrever um mini-doc novo, por exemplo `docs/design/exportacao-de-relatorios-armazenamento-s3.md`, que cita o original, diz o que mudou e por quê, e traz os próprios trade-offs.

O motivo você já deu: com o segundo worker, o download caía no worker sem o arquivo e devolvia 404. Antes de escrever, preciso de algumas respostas, porque não dá pra deduzir nenhuma delas:

1. **Quando a mudança entrou em produção?** O original foi atualizado em 2026-03-03. Você disse "desde março", mas não sei a data da troca pro S3.
2. **Como o download funciona agora?** O original diz que o `GET /exports/<job_id>/download` era servido pelo worker lendo o disco. Agora o worker lê do S3 e devolve, a API devolve uma URL pré-assinada, ou outra coisa?
